KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread rain arrives Friday and continues Fri 
night before tapering off early Sat. Rain will be heavy at times 
Fri/Fri night across RI, southeast MA including Cape Cod and the 
Islands. 

Warm advection (WAA) pattern has resulted in overcast conditions 
across the region this afternoon, along with an impressive warm 
sector airmass for early Nov, with dew pts in the low 60s across the 
area. The combination of clouds and high dew pts will result in a 
very mild night ahead by early Nov standards, with min temps only 
in the low 60s. This will likely result in record warm min temps 
tonight. See the climate section below for details. 

Rain becomes more widespread Friday, especially during the 
afternoon, along with rain heavy at times across RI and southeast 
MA, continuing into Fri night. RRQ of 100+ kt upper level jet streak 
over SNE helps spin up a frontal wave that tracks along or near the 
south coast Fri night. Copious deep layer moisture available with 
dew pts in the low to mid 60s, PWATs up to +3 sigma and some weak 
instability (MU Capes 500-750 j/kg) to enhance the rainfall. In 
addition, surface wave will be accompanied by a 40-45 kt low level 
SSW jet, enhancing the low level convergence. Still some uncertainty 
on the exact axis of heaviest rainfall, but all guidance suggest 
somewhere over RI and southeast MA, including Cape Cod and the 
Islands. The development of the surface wave will result in a nearly 
stationary frontal boundary, increasing the risk for 
flooding from training cells.

New 12z Hi Res guid simulating 3-5" rainfall across RI and southeast 
MA, along with support from the 00z global ens offering low probs of 
4+ inches. Thus, high confidence for 1-3" with lower probs for 
isolated 4-5". This would result in potential urban/poor drainage 
flooding, including the typical flood prone areas of New Bedford, 
Fall River, Providence, Cranston, etc. Given the time of year, leaf 
clogged drains will only exacerbate the urban/poor drainage flood 
potential. Regarding small rivers and streams in RI and southeast 
MA, 4+ inches would be required for minor flooding. Hence, looking 
more like a poor drainage/urban flood potential. Elsewhere across CT 
into northern MA, less rainfall is expected. Thus, the flood threat 
is limited to RI and southeast MA. Given the flood potential and 
uncertainty in the exact location of heaviest rainfall, we will 
hoist a flood watch to message the threat for flooding. 

Rainfall probs initially fall off Saturday morning with a lull 
in the precipitation. Will see a resurgence in precipitation 
probabilities Saturday afternoon as the cold core of an upper 
level low moves overhead lowering 500mb temps to around -20C. 
The anomalously cold air aloft paired with partial clearing at 
the surface likely results in steep lapse rates and widespread 
showers. A few showers may be capable of producing heavy 
rainfall and small hail as strong cold air advection cools the 
mid levels of the atmosphere. The strong cold advection will be 
most evident at 850 mb as temperatures fall from +9-10C Saturday
morning to +1-4C by Saturday night. Guidance depicts surface 
low pressure developing in the Gulf of Maine Saturday night into
Sunday. Currently have the highest POPs along and N of the Mass
Pike for Sunday as cool cyclonic flow enhances rainfall chances
further to the N. Overall it looks to be a raw weekend between 
the scattered to widespread showers and high temperatures in the
mid 50s to upper 60s. 

A series of fronts then move across southern New England next week. 
However, limited moisture should only mean periods of clouds at 
times and mainly dry weather.
